newsitem.title: USA: Old people too slow for most traffic lights.
newsitem.headline: Old people too slow for most traffic lights.

text.p: Only one elderly person in 100 manages to cross the street in the time allocated by traffic lights, researchers said Thursday, saying old people should be given more time.

Although some old people can hurry to get across safely, many who have had strokes or other illnesses or injuries cannot. The elderly have the highest rate of pedestrian death and injury in the United States.

To reduce the risk, communities should modify traffic signals to allow people to get across the street safely, wrote National Institute of Ageing researcher Jean Langlois and collegues in the current edition of the American Journal of Public Health.
The researchers tracked old people in New Haven, Conn., for seven years and then gave them a road test.
From a standing position, people over age 72 were asked to walk to the other end of an eight-foot course at their normal speed. They could use canes, walkers or other devices.
Only five of 989 people tested -- less than one percent -- walked at least 4 feet-per-second, the speed generally required to get across the street before the light changes to red.
About seven percent could move at a rate of three feet- per-second, which is how the crossing lights are timed in sections of New Haven with substantial senior populations.

About one in 10 surveyed reported that they had trouble crossing the street. Many had slow walking speeds, poor vision, lower mental status scores on tests and a need for help in day-to-day activities.
